claims.text: The target material is an as-designed, high-performance, multicomponent high-entropy alloy.
Adding a small amount of WC will reduce post-exposure toughness degradation in the HEA.
The proposed intervention is the addition of a small amount of WC.
The relevant thermal-exposure range is 600–1000 °C for 100 hours.
WC addition will produce a stable solid-solution structure.
WC particles will be dispersed within the alloy microstructure.
Dispersed WC particles will obstruct dislocation movement.
Dispersed WC particles will reduce the formation of deleterious intermetallic phases.
Dispersed WC particles will reduce grain coarsening during thermal exposure.
Suppressing deleterious intermetallic formation and grain coarsening will retain alloy toughness.
The WC-added alloy will retain at least 80% toughness relative to the untreated baseline after exposure.
The comparison baseline is an untreated HEA with the same composition and processing history.
The proposed loading boundary is up to 500 MPa.
The exact WC amount and optimal processing conditions are uncertain.
Post-exposure toughness can be compared by Charpy impact testing of WC-added and untreated specimens.
TEM and SEM can be used to compare the post-exposure microstructures of the two specimen groups.
The hypothesis is falsified if the WC-added HEA does not have significantly higher toughness than the untreated baseline.

contradictions.description: Adding WC changes composition, so a WC-added alloy cannot be compared with an untreated baseline that has literally the same composition. The baseline should instead match the original matrix composition and processing history apart from WC addition and any processing strictly required for it.

Retention of at least 80% 'compared to the untreated baseline' does not necessarily mean toughness is significantly higher than the untreated baseline, whereas the falsification rule requires a significant improvement. The reference for the 80% retention threshold is also ambiguous.
